items.title: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
items.summary:
UK statement comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single…
items.t: Andy Burnham in Brussels as UK and EU close in on Brexit reset deal – live

items.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
items.summary:
In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is…
items.t: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins

items.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
items.summary:
The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market

  • Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start.

Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja. Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries wins overwhelming Speaker-designate vote as progressives' revolt falls flat
items.summary:
Democrats are fretting that the "Bloc" of progressives will lug House Democrats to the left.

But, there is strength in numbers.

Yours truly wanted to understand just how much sway progressives might have over the House Democratic Caucus. Look no further than Wednesday morning’s vote for speaker.

No one challenged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to become speaker-designate in the internal caucus vote.

It’s about the math.

Jeffries marshaled 251 of the 262 secret ballots cast. The recorded vote revealed that despite all of their noise and clamor, extreme progressives really don’t have much juice compared to the rest of the Democratic Caucus. In fact, rank-and-file Democrats crushed their progressive colleagues.

Democrats did not vote by name. But numbers say a lot. While the recorded vote could have revealed potential craters of dissent among Democrats and questions about Jeffries, the tally registered the opposite. It showed just how diminutive the hard left is in the Democratic Caucus.

JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER'

Do they exude an outsized political voice? Yes. But success in Congress is measured in numbers.…

items.title: ASRA Q. NOMANI: Inside the coordinated activist blitz that crashed Anthropic’s historic Nasdaq debut
items.summary:
As Anthropic executives gathered inside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square on Thursday morning to ring the opening bell for a historic $81 billion initial public offering, a tightly orchestrated coalition of far-left, socialist, environmental, anti-Israel and Democratic grassroots groups executed a staged street action outside, complete with linked-arm sit-ins, pre-printed banners and rapid-fire social media drops timed to hijack the news cycle.

"This IPO has got to go! Hey, hey, ho, ho," the staged protesters chanted to a small cadre of photographers as the audience.

"Shame! Shame!" a protester yelled to a few responding "Shame!" in response.

items.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
items.summary:
The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech

It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for…

The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.

items.title: Should JD Vance run for president? I say go for it, habibi! | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it

How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?

I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.
